period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: Kite Watching: First Look at the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.141): pre-reading oral activation — personal kite experiences.
Let us read (p.141): picture-completion fill-in using given word list.

time_bands.activity: Open with the pre-reading discussion from “Let us read” (p.141): invite students to share whether they have flown or seen a kite, where, and what they noticed. Encourage brief, vivid descriptions of colour, shape, and tail design.
Read the poem aloud, teacher-led with students following in their books (pp.141–142). Pause after each stanza to let the image settle; use a gentle, lilting pace that mirrors the poem's own rhythm.

Work through the picture-completion activity from “Let us read” (p.141): students fill in blanks using the given words (windy, kite, flying, birds, sky, looking, has ribbons), then share two things they would add to the picture and complete the “If I were the child / kite” prompts orally.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem opens with a child observing kites that look “Like coloured birds” — this simile is the poem’s first literary device and worth a brief pause even in this first encounter. Students who have not flown kites personally should still find the picture-completion task accessible, as it anchors imaginative responses to a visual prompt rather than lived experience.

periods.activity_title: True, False and the Truth About Simile

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.143): mark eleven statements True or False after silent reading.
Let us discuss (p.143): complete simile sentences and discuss their imaginative effect.

time_bands.activity: Students re-read the poem silently (pp.141–142), keeping pencils ready to mark the True/False statements from “Let us discuss” (p.143). Allow an unhurried reading aloud.
Go through all eleven True/False statements together as a class, asking students to point to the line in the poem that confirms or contradicts each statement before writing their verdict.

Move to the simile activity from “Let us discuss” (p.143): students complete the sentences about ‘Like coloured birds’ and ‘light as air’, then share whether simile helps them imagine better — a quick paired exchange before one or two pairs report to the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem aloud once, students now engage with its literal truth-claims before its figurative language. A common pitfall is that students mark statement 6 (“The kite is made of cloth and plastic”) as true by assumption — the poem says ‘paper wings’, and the transcript confirms paper kites go back to ancient Indian tradition; nudge students to use the poem’s own words as evidence.

periods.activity_title: Sound and Pattern: Alliteration, Repetition, Rhyme

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.144): identify alliteration, repetition, and rhyme scheme stanza by stanza.
Let us think and reflect (p.144–145): analyse stanza 4 lines and identify aerial viewpoint.

time_bands.activity: Work through the alliteration, repetition, and rhyme tasks from “Let us discuss” (p.144): students find the consonant-sound pairs in stanzas 1 and 3, identify the repeated words in the final stanza, then underline rhyming end-words and circle the non-rhyming ones across all five stanzas.

Turn to “Let us think and reflect” (p.144–145): read the stanza 4 lines together (“What fun it would be / To look right down”), then tackle the word-feeling question and the aerial viewpoint question as a guided class discussion.
Close by reading the whole poem once more as a class, this time students joining in on the rhyming lines — an enjoyable consolidation of the sound-pattern work just completed.

periods.teacher_notes: The ABCB rhyme scheme means the first and third lines of each stanza do not rhyme — students often circle all four end-words in a stanza rather than just the non-rhyming ones; model stanza 1 on the board before asking them to work independently. The repetition of ‘high, high’ in the final line is the poem’s emotional peak, and the appreciation summary notes it emphasises both elevation and wonder.

periods.activity_title: Imagining High: Deeper Questions on the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.145): answer four extended questions on the poem’s imagery and perspective.

time_bands.activity: Open with a brief re-read of stanzas 4 and 5 (pp.141–142), teacher-led, to refresh the aerial images before moving into extended response questions.

Students work through the extended questions from “Let us think and reflect” (p.145): how the poet describes kites in the first two lines; what songs the child hears flying on the kite; why people stare and what feelings that might stir; and what a kite carrying the child might say. Pairs discuss briefly before students write individual responses.
Invite two or three students to share their answers to the final question (what the kite would tell the child) — a brief, open sharing that celebrates imaginative thinking before the class moves on.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem’s tone is exhilarated and playful, with a gentle irony in the final stanza where the child imagines others wishing they were ‘high, high in the air’ — students who grasp this reversal will produce richer answers to the ‘why people stare’ question. The question about why the child needs to climb a tree is a comprehension trap: the poem does not mention this at all, so accept any honest, text-supported response. Tasks not covered in class — the kite-festival internet video task (p.141) — may be explored independently at home.

periods.activity_title: Listening to the Kite Festival: Facts in the Air

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.148): circle incorrect words while listening, then rewrite the correct words.

time_bands.activity: Set the context: tell students they will hear a short talk about Kite Festivals in India. Ask students to open their books to p.148 and read the seven statements once silently so they know what to listen for.
Read the transcript aloud clearly (p.163) as students listen and circle the words they think are incorrect. Maintain a natural speaking pace — do not slow down or emphasise clues.
Read the transcript a second time. Students now confirm or revise their circles and write the correct replacement words beside each statement in their books.

Go through all seven statements together: for each one, ask a student to name the word they circled and the word they replaced it with, then confirm against the transcript. Briefly discuss which festivals and states were named in the talk.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript states the festival is celebrated in ‘Western India’ (not Eastern) and during ‘January’ (not June) — these are the two most commonly confused facts; listen for students who circle no words on the true statements, which means they are not distinguishing fact from assumption. The talk also mentions Karnataka’s Tourism Department organises the festival ‘once each year’, which the textbook statement renders as ‘every year’ — both are correct; accept either.

periods.activity_title: Speaking From Experience, Writing From Imagination

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.149): narrate a personal kite-flying or kite-watching experience in complete sentences.
Let us write (p.149): plan and draft a 100-word paragraph titled ‘I am a Kite’.

time_bands.activity: Speaking task from “Let us speak” (p.149): students take one minute to organise their thoughts (where, when, why, how), then five or six volunteers narrate their kite experience to the class in complete sentences. Prompt hesitant speakers with the four question words.

Bridge to writing: in pairs, students discuss the hints from “Let us write” (p.149) — shape, colours, parts, location, owner, activities, friends, message for humans — making quick notes. Keep this a quick paired exchange, not a long planning phase.

Students write their 100-word paragraph titled ‘I am a Kite’ individually in their notebooks. Circulate and give brief formative nudges on first-person voice and sentence variety. Students do a quick self-read and make one correction before the close.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have not flown a kite may narrate the experience of watching one fly — the task explicitly allows this, so affirm it clearly before the speaking round begins. In the writing phase, a common drift is into third-person narration (‘the kite flies’ rather than ‘I fly’); a brief model sentence on the board (‘I am a diamond-shaped kite with a long red tail’) helps students stay in the first-person voice the task requires.

periods.activity_title: Words That Move: Parts, Poems, and Kite Vocabulary

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.146): fill in a dialogue using parts-of-a-kite vocabulary (tail, cover, spine, line, reel, nose).
Let us learn (p.148): circle drift-movement words; describe movement words glide, dive, soar, swoop, circle.

time_bands.activity: Study the labelled kite diagram at p.146 together, then students complete the Bina–Saroj dialogue by filling in the six blanks (tail, cover, spine, line, reel, nose). Compare answers in pairs before a whole-class check.

From “Let us learn” (p.148): students circle the words that match the ‘drift’ movement (slow, float, etc.) and justify their choices briefly. Then read the five movement words — glide, dive, soar, swoop, circle — and students describe the type of movement each suggests, drawing on the poem’s own imagery where helpful.

Pairs compose one sentence each using two of the five movement words in the context of the poem’s world, then share with the class. This rounds off the vocabulary work with a short, creative application.

periods.teacher_notes: The kite-parts vocabulary (nose, spine, cover, line, reel, tail) is domain-specific and may be unfamiliar — let the labelled diagram do the work before the dialogue task, rather than asking students to guess cold. The distinction between ‘drift’ (slow, floating) and ‘soar’ or ‘swoop’ (directional, energetic) is the conceptual heart of the movement-word task; the poem itself uses both ‘fly’ and ‘drift’ and can anchor the discussion. The cinquain task (p.147) is rich but requires more time than is available here; it is flagged as self-study for interested students.

periods.activity_title: From Ancient Gathas to Kite-Making: Exploring Kite Culture

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.149–150): explore kite types, discuss which is most common, research and plan steps to make a kite.

time_bands.activity: Share the cultural note from “Let us explore” (p.149): kites appear in the thirteenth-century Marathi poetry of saint Namadeva, who called them ‘gudi’ and described them as made from ‘kaagad’ (paper). Students briefly discuss what this reveals about kites as a long-standing cultural tradition.

Look at the five kite types (Parafoil, Delta, Rokkaku, Diamond-shaped, Box kite) from “Let us explore” (p.150). Students individually choose the type most commonly seen in their area and share their reasoning. In groups, students then discuss and list the steps needed to make a simple diamond kite, drawing on any prior knowledge.

Each group shares their step-list with the class; the teacher compiles a master sequence on the board. Students copy the steps and sketch a simple plan of their intended kite — shape, colour, and the message they would write on it. This in-class plan is complete in itself; no artefact from outside is required.

periods.teacher_notes: The connection between Namadeva’s thirteenth-century ‘gudi’ and the paper-winged kite of the poem grounds the beyond-text exploration in the chapter’s own cultural thread. Students who have made kites before are a valuable resource for the step-listing discussion — invite them to lead their group rather than only the most verbally confident student.

periods.activity_title: The Whole Poem in One Flight: Synthesis and Celebration

time_bands.activity: Whole-class re-read of the poem (pp.141–142), teacher and students alternating stanzas. As each stanza is read, one student names one literary device or language feature the class has explored — simile, alliteration, repetition, rhyme scheme, movement vocabulary — in any order.

Structured oral round: each student prepares and delivers two or three sentences that bring together two threads from the chapter — for example, connecting the poem’s ‘paper wings’ to the cultural history of paper kites, or linking the ‘wild wind’ alliteration to the movement words studied. Brief, focused contributions from as many students as possible.

Small groups create a short collective statement: ‘What makes this poem about kites also a poem about imagination?’ Each group writes two sentences on the board. The class reads all the statements and discusses which ideas appear across groups.
Close with a final reading of the last stanza aloud together, emphasising the repeated ‘high, high in the air’ — a joyful, shared ending that honours the poem’s own exhilarated tone.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws on the poem’s full arc — from the opening observation of kites as coloured birds, through the child’s fantasy of flight, to the gentle irony of the final stanza where those below wish to be ‘high, high in the air.’ The synthesis question about imagination invites students to articulate why a poem about a simple childhood activity carries a larger emotional charge — the appreciation summary describes the tone as ‘exhilarated and playful’, which is a useful anchor phrase for the discussion.

items.source_lo: Student reads, discusses and analyses a poem using its imagery, literary devices and structure as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Daphne Lister’s five-stanza fantasy-of-flight poem; simile, alliteration, repetition, ABCB rhyme; aerial viewpoint.
items.item_stem: Read the opening lines of the poem beginning “Up in the air”. Which of the following correctly identifies the simile the poet uses to describe the kites?

options.label: A
options.text: The kites are compared to coloured birds because they fly high and look bright against the sky.

options.label: B
options.text: The kites are compared to paper wings because they are made of paper.

options.label: C
options.text: The kites are compared to rooftops because the child sees them from above.

options.label: D
options.text: The kites are compared to the wild wind because they move quickly.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses the vehicle of the simile (coloured birds) with the material the kite is made from (paper wings).
what_each_option_reveals.D: Misidentifies alliteration — ‘wild wind’ — as the comparison device rather than the simile in stanza 1.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Conflates the aerial viewpoint in stanza 4 with the simile in stanza 1, showing confusion of poetic sections.

items.source_lo: Student reads, discusses and analyses a poem using its imagery, literary devices and structure as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Daphne Lister’s five-stanza fantasy-of-flight poem; simile, alliteration, repetition, ABCB rhyme; aerial viewpoint.
items.item_stem: In the final stanza of the poem, the child imagines looking down while the people below “stand and stare.” What does this reversal — where the child is now the one in the sky while others wish they were up there — reveal about the central feeling the poem is building towards? Refer to at least one other stanza in your answer.

expected_elements: Names the reversal: child imagined below becomes the one envied above.
Links to an earlier stanza expressing the child’s wish to fly.
Identifies the poem’s dominant feeling as wonder, triumph, or joyful fantasy.
Uses at least one word or phrase from the poem as evidence.

items.source_lo: Student listens critically to an informational talk and identifies factual errors by comparing spoken content with written statements.
items.source_context: Spoken talk on Kite Festival: Makar Sankranti, Uttarayan, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Telangana, Karnataka, Punjab, Independence Day.
items.item_stem: Listen to the talk about Kite Festivals in India. Then read the statements below and mark each one True or False.

options.text: People in India also fly kites to celebrate Independence Day.
The Kite Festival in India takes place during Makar Sankranti in the month of January.
Uttarayan is the name given to the Kite Festival in Eastern India.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the talk states Makar Sankranti falls in January.
2. False — the talk says Uttarayan is celebrated in Western India, not Eastern India.
3. True — the talk explicitly mentions kite-flying on Independence Day.

items.source_lo: Student listens critically to an informational talk and identifies factual errors by comparing spoken content with written statements.
items.source_context: Spoken talk on Kite Festival: Makar Sankranti, Uttarayan, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Telangana, Karnataka, Punjab, Independence Day.
items.item_stem: The speaker in the talk names several Indian states where the Kite Festival is celebrated. Based on what you heard, write the names of three states mentioned by the speaker, and for one of them, explain what the speaker said about how or when the festival is celebrated there.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Any three from: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Telangana, Karnataka, Punjab. A valid explanation for one — for example: Gujarat is the main centre of celebrations for Uttarayan; or Karnataka’s Tourism Department organises the Kite Festival once each year; or Punjab celebrates with kites during Baisakhi and Basant Panchami.

items.item_stem: Describe to the class a time you flew a kite or watched someone fly one. Tell your classmates where it happened, what the kite looked like, and what you did. Speak in complete sentences.

expected_elements: Names a place and occasion for the kite experience.
Describes the kite’s appearance with at least one detail.
Recounts at least one action taken or observed.
Uses complete sentences throughout.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are the child in the poem — riding high on a kite, looking down over the park and the rooftops of town. In two or three sentences, tell the class what you see and how you feel, and give one reason why you would — or would not — want to stay up there.

expected_elements: Adopts the first-person voice of the child in the poem.
Describes at least one thing seen from above (park, rooftops, people).
States a feeling with a reason drawn from the poem’s imagery.
Gives a clear opinion on staying up or coming down with a reason.

items.item_stem: A kite shop has asked for a short notice to display on its window. Write a notice of about 40–50 words in the voice of a kite, describing yourself — your shape, your colours, and one special thing about you — and inviting a child to choose you. Use the first person (I, my).

expected_elements: Written in first person throughout (I, my, me).
Names the kite’s shape and at least one colour.
Includes one appealing detail — tail, message, special part.
Ends with an invitation directed at a child reader.

items.item_stem: Write a paragraph of about 80–100 words in the first person, imagining you are a kite flying over your town on a windy afternoon. Include: what you look like, who is holding your string, what you can see from up high, who your sky-friends are, and what message you would send down to the people below.

expected_elements: Sustained first-person voice throughout the paragraph.
Describes appearance and at least one aerial observation.
Names or imagines sky-companions (birds, other kites, wind).
Ends with a message or thought directed at people below.
Writes in mostly complete sentences with varied description.

items.item_stem: Match each part of a kite in Column A with its correct description in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A (Part) | Column B (Description) |
|---|---|
| Tail | The tip at the very top of the kite |
| Reel | The flat surface that catches the wind |
| Nose | The long strip that helps the kite balance in the air |
| Cover | The spool on which the flying line is wound |
| Spine | The central stick that runs along the length of the kite |

answer_key.right: The long strip that helps the kite balance in the air
The spool on which the flying line is wound
The tip at the very top of the kite
The flat surface that catches the wind
The central stick that runs along the length of the kite

items.source_lo: Student applies domain vocabulary and movement-word distinctions drawn from the section’s language in context.
items.source_context: Parts of a kite (nose, spine, cover, line, reel, tail); movement words fly, drift, glide, dive, soar, swoop, circle.
items.item_stem: The poem uses the word ‘drift’ to describe how the child moves on the kite’s paper wings. Choose two movement words from the list below that best share the same quality of movement as ‘drift’, and write one sentence for each chosen word showing how a kite or bird might move in that way.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Acceptable choices are ‘glide’ and ‘circle’ — both share drift’s quality of slow, smooth, unhurried movement, unlike ‘dive’ or ‘swoop’ which are sharp and fast. Sentences should place the chosen word in a kite or bird context with a plausible image.

items.source_lo: Student connects a literary text to its cultural and historical context and extends learning through hands-on exploration.
items.source_context: Namadeva’s thirteenth-century ‘gudi’ kites; kite types (Parafoil, Delta, Rokkaku, Diamond, Box); kite-making steps and message.
items.item_stem: The poem describes a kite as having ‘paper wings.’ The text also mentions that the thirteenth-century Marathi poet Namadeva called a kite a ‘gudi’ and described it as made from ‘kaagad’ — the Marathi word for paper. Write a paragraph of about 60–80 words explaining what this historical detail tells us about kites in Indian culture, and why you think a poet writing hundreds of years ago and a modern poet like Daphne Lister might both have found kites worth writing about.

expected_elements: Identifies that kites have been part of Indian culture for centuries.
Notes the shared material — paper — across centuries and cultures.
Gives at least one reason why kites inspire poets (freedom, joy, flight).
Writes in mostly complete sentences of appropriate length.

items.source_lo: Student connects a literary text to its cultural and historical context and extends learning through hands-on exploration.
items.source_context: Namadeva’s thirteenth-century ‘gudi’ kites; kite types (Parafoil, Delta, Rokkaku, Diamond, Box); kite-making steps and message.
items.item_stem: Design and make a simple paper kite. Your project must include: (1) a sketch or the actual kite showing its shape and colours; (2) a written list of the steps you followed to make it; (3) a message of no more than ten words written on the kite. Bring your kite to class and explain in two or three sentences why you chose that shape and what message you wrote.

expected_elements: Kite or sketch present with shape and colour visible.
Step list is sequenced and has at least four steps.
Message is present and within the ten-word limit.
Oral explanation names the shape choice and message intention.
